Hi Mateo,

Thanks again for the demo last week — CatalystWorks is excited about moving a portion of our inference traffic onto Redwood Dedicated. Before we sign the SOW we need to validate a couple of operational things so our SREs can sign off:

Raj — great to hear and thanks for the data.

We can definitely walk through this tomorrow. High level answers to set expectations ahead of the call:

- Cushion guidance: for sustained 95th percentile workloads we typically recommend 25–40% cushion on top of measured peak QPS; for spiky 99th percentile workloads we recommend 40–90% depending on acceptable cost vs latency tradeoffs.
- Eviction behavior: Dedicated pools will attempt to route to shoulder pools or trigger transient burst where configured; if capacity is exhausted we have a prioritized eviction policy (customer-tagged pools first, then opportunistic jobs) and a graceful throttle with 503 + Retry-After. We will share the exact SLA impact and evicted-job heuristics in the runbook.
- Autoscale: default scale-up is fast (30–90s depending on model warming/kv-cache rebuild) and scale-down uses a cool-down (10–30m) to avoid oscillation. For customers on reserved slabs we can enforce minimum slab commitments (1–4 hours) to reduce churn.

I attached a small capacity template (CatalystWorks sheet) — fill the traffic columns and we can run a baseline sizing with recommended cushion across both static slab + shoulder pools.

If the 11am PT slot works I’ll send a calendar invite.

Best,
Mateo Alvarez
Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference

Mateo — excellent summary. Drafting quick runbook below you can share on the call; I also attached the ops playbook and linked a drive doc with historical cushion numbers from similar customers.

1) Cushion guidance (short):
- 95th profile (steady peaks): default 30% cushion on measured peak slots. This balances cost & tail latency; empirically keeps 95th-latency within target for M2-like families.
- 99th/spiky profile: start at 60% cushion, and consider an ephemeral shoulder pool with 15–20% additional headroom for extreme short spikes.

2) Eviction ordering and SLA implications (short):
- Order: opportunistic jobs (batch/low-priority) -> shoulder/ephemeral slab fallback -> reserved-slab throttling -> customer slab eviction (last resort).
- SLA: if we fail to place requests, we surface 503 with Retry-After; an incident-level SLA breach is only declared when persistent evictions last > 5m and error rate rises > 2% above baseline. We can include this language in the SOW.

3) Autoscale params (short):
- Scale-up: target 45s median for model types that warm kv-cache fast; allocate extra warm-up tokens to reduce tail (~30–90s range).
- Scale-down: 20m cool-down to reduce oscillation; minimum slab reservation for dedicated customers 1 hour (negotiable).

4) Practical knobs to offer the customer on the call:
- Cushion % (customer-chosen: conservative/ balanced/ aggressive) with expected cost delta estimates.
- Shoulder pool size as % of reserved slab (0/10/20%).
- Minimum slab duration (1h/4h) to control billing churn.
- Eviction preference tags for their own jobs to prefer throttling over full preemption.

Links: https://drive.redwood.com/drive/folders/1a2b3C_CatalystWorks-Runbooks
